Why: Both sap and root hairs are vital transportation systems that move the glucose and oxygen required for cellular respiration to every plant cell, ensuring the maintenance of homeostasis.

Strategies for Survival in Different Animal Species

When bluefin tuna reach breeding age, they migrate in schools until they reach an area in the ocean where conditions are right. Bluefin tuna then spawn, where they release millions of eggs and sperm into the water.

Spawning takes place in nutrient-poor water. Young tuna practice cannibalism to obtain nutrients. Once the young reach a certain size, they stop eating each other and travel in schools to other regions of the ocean. Only two out of every 30 million fertilized eggs will reach adulthood. Four to six years later they will spawn, and the cycle will begin all over again.
question:
Which piece of evidence best supports how the tuna's spawning behavior provides a survival advantage?

(Biology August 2025)
options: If a pathogen infects some of the fish in the school during spawning, then others will most likely become infected.
Due to the large number of fish, the school must move from one area to another because food quickly runs out.
It is more likely that many offspring will be hatched, increasing the likelihood that some will reproduce.
If there are many fish in one area, wastes accumulate more quickly, and oxygen levels decrease.
explanation:
Passage Excerpt: 'Bluefin tuna then spawn, where they release millions of eggs and sperm into the water... Only two out of every 30 million fertilized eggs will reach adulthood.'

Why: Releasing millions of eggs at once is an evolutionary survival strategy. By overwhelming the environment with offspring, it guarantees that despite massive predation and high mortality rates, at least a few will successfully reach adulthood and reproduce.

options: Shrews lay millions of eggs underground to ensure at least some survive predation.
The caravan makes it possible for the shrews to be better protected as they move from place to place, increasing their survival chances through parental care.
Shrews abandon their young immediately after birth to avoid attracting predators to the nest.
The mother shrew practices cannibalism on the weakest offspring to ensure the strongest survive.

Relevant Diagram:

Why: Unlike tuna that abandon their young, shrews invest heavily in parental care, providing milk and moving offspring in protective caravans. This behavior results in a much higher offspring survival rate (about 50%), compensating for their smaller litter sizes.

question:
Explain how the process of evolution has led to the development of this behavior in bison populations.

(Biology August 2025)
options: Bison intentionally learned to form circles to trap their prey, passing this acquired skill to offspring.
When threatened, the male and female bison form a protective circle around the calves, increasing the chances that the calves will survive and pass on this adaptation to future generations.
The process of evolution slowly mutated the bison's DNA during an attack, instantly creating this behavior.
Predators selectively hunted bison that stood in circles, causing solitary bison to survive and reproduce more effectively.
explanation:
Passage Excerpt: 'When predators... threaten the calves, the adults form a double ring around the calves.'

Why: Evolution operates on natural selection. Bison that exhibited this protective circular behavior effectively shielded their young from predators. These surviving calves then grew up to reproduce and pass the genetic basis for this advantageous behavior down to subsequent generations.

question:
In the 1800s, unregulated hunting reduced bison herds from tens of millions of individuals to fewer than 1,000. How might the DNA of the modern bison populations compare with the DNA of ancestral populations prior to the 1800s?

(Biology August 2025)
options: Modern bison have more genetic diversity than their ancestors as a result of an increase in available mates.
Modern bison have less genetic diversity than the population before the 1800s did as a result of increased random mutations.
The DNA of the modern bison is identical to that of bison living before the 1800s because they all evolved from the same common ancestor.
The DNA of modern bison shows less genetic diversity compared to their ancestors due to the limited genetic variation remaining in their population.
explanation:
Passage Excerpt: '...reduced bison herds from tens of millions of individuals to fewer than 1,000.'

Why: When a population undergoes a massive reduction (a population bottleneck), an enormous amount of unique DNA variations are permanently lost when those individuals die. The surviving modern descendants are rebuilt from this extremely limited gene pool, resulting in severely restricted genetic diversity compared to their ancestors.

A Unique Relationship: Mulberries and Silk

The ability of living organisms to rearrange elements into different forms and groups is fundamental to life. Mulberry plants use specific biological processes to combine molecules present in the environment in order to produce the substances they need to carry out life functions. Silkworms eat mulberry leaves exclusively, getting all of their water and other nutrients from these leaves.

Most nutrients from the mulberry leaves enter the silkworm in the form of macromolecules. The macromolecules must be metabolized by body systems of the silkworm into a form that the cells of the worm are able to use. The model below summarizes some of the processes the silkworm uses to convert the nutrient macromolecules from the mulberry tree into a usable form.

Cellular respiration within the cells of the mulberry tree breaks the bonds of glucose to release amino acids, a usable source of cellular energy.
Digestion within the cells of the silkworm breaks the bonds of glucose to release amino acids that can be used to build ATP for energy.
Digestion within the cells of the mulberry tree breaks the bonds of glucose to release elements that can be used to build lipids for energy.

Why: The model illustrates glucose being metabolized into ATP inside the silkworm. This is the definition of cellular respiration: breaking down the chemical bonds in glucose to synthesize ATP, the primary usable energy currency of the cell.

Ivory and Elephants

In African elephant populations, both males and females usually have ivory tusks, which are actually a pair of massive teeth. Some females never grow them. Tusks are crucial to male elephants for defense and in their competition for mates. In many parts of the world, elephant ivory is still viewed as a status symbol. It was used to produce small carvings, jewelry, piano keys, and chess sets. Traditional medicine used ivory powder to treat a variety of illnesses. Conflict between humans and elephants exists across Africa. As human populations grow, people are moving into wild areas, increasing loss of natural habitats. Elephants compete with people for decreasing resources. Elephants searching for food frequently enter villages and sometimes damage property, uproot vegetable gardens, and can harm people. Multiple organizations have come up with solutions to reduce conflict between elephants and humans, as described below.

Solution One: Beehive Fences
Beehive fences are made by hanging beehives connected by wire around crops to deter elephants from entering areas by using their natural fear of African honeybees. When an elephant pushes the wire the hives shake, alerting guard bees which then defend their hives. Over time, elephants learn to avoid these bee-fenced areas.

Millions of acres of elephant habitat are set aside where limited elephant hunting is allowed. These areas are closely monitored and regulated. Without this managed hunting, the critically important elephant range will be lost to other land uses.

Driving the Florida Panther to Extinction

The decline in the Florida panther population is an example of how humans have had an impact on the biodiversity of an area. The panther is a large cat that preys primarily upon wild hogs, raccoons, and deer. They can be found in forested areas, pinelands, and freshwater swamp forests.

During the 1800s and early 1900s, habitat loss and hunting led to the panther's near-extinction. By the mid-1980s, only 20 to 30 panthers could be found in the wild. Conservation efforts to increase the panther population started with the release of eight females from Texas in 1995 into available panther habitat in south Florida, much of which was protected from human activity. The Florida panther population historically bordered the Texas population, with interbreeding occurring naturally. Such conservation efforts have succeeded in bringing the wild panther population up to about 200 individuals.

(Biology August 2025)
options: The average panther reproductive rate will increase in order to maintain the panther population.
If their territory decreases because of housing developments, it will become easier for the males to find genetically diverse mates.
Due to the size of the population, genetic variation is most likely low, decreasing the ability of the panther population to adapt to environmental changes.
The panther population has rebounded and will most likely continue to rise, regardless of changes to their habitat.
explanation:
Passage Excerpt: 'By the mid-1980s, only 20 to 30 panthers could be found in the wild... succeeded in bringing the wild panther population up to about 200 individuals.'

Why: The population went through a severe bottleneck.
